opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've been thinking about a lot. My view is that tokenization isn't really a side detail. It's closely tied to what the Transformer is actually good at.

Attention works best when each token is a fairly meaningful unit of information. When you attend over a sequence, every position can look directly at every other position, and you pay quadratically for that. That's a great deal when each token carries a lot of semantic content, like a word or a chunk of a word. It's much less efficient when the units are very fine-grained, like raw bytes or characters, where any single element doesn't mean much on its own. So the tokenizer is a compression step done before the model ever sees the data. It turns the raw signal into something closer to the level of abstraction where attention shines.

That's why Transformers have leaned so heavily on tokenizers. If you run them on raw bytes, the sequences get several times longer, compute blows up, and empirically they tend to do worse at matched compute. The tokenizer hides a weakness of the architecture.

But tokenizers bring their own problems. They're hand-designed heuristics, usually something like BPE, and they're trained separately from the model and then frozen. That causes a lot of strange behavior: trouble with spelling and character-level tasks, inconsistent handling of numbers, worse performance on languages and domains underrepresented when the tokenizer was built, and sensitivity to small formatting changes like whitespace. And for modalities like DNA, audio or other raw signals, there often isn't any natural tokenization at all.

So my takeaway is that the tokenizer matters so much because it's doing real modeling work, deciding how to chunk the data into meaningful units, and we're doing that part by hand instead of learning it. A lot of my interest, both with state space models and more recent work, is in architectures that handle fine-grained, uncompressed data more gracefully and can learn their own chunking end to end. Then the model decides what the right units are, instead of us fixing them in advance with a heuristic.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization matters and shapes the model’s input, but does not describe a shift from separate word-level and character-level regimes to treating tokenization as a model hyperparameter.

r002.rationale: It says attention works best when each token is a meaningful unit and argues that Transformers benefit from tokenizers that create such units.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that tokenization matters because Transformers are, in a sense, kind of weak at the thing tokenization is doing for them. If you think about what a tokenizer does, it's taking raw bytes or characters and compressing them into these chunks, these tokens, that the model then operates on. And the reason we do that is partly efficiency, right? Attention is quadratic in sequence length, so if you can shrink your sequence by a factor of four or five by working over tokens instead of bytes, that's a huge win.

But I'd argue the deeper reason is that the Transformer architecture itself isn't great at doing that compression on its own. Attention is really good at retrieving and comparing discrete, meaningful units. It's not as naturally suited to taking a long stream of low-level, fairly uninformative symbols and aggregating them into something higher level. So tokenization is essentially a hand-engineered preprocessing step that does that aggregation for the model before it ever sees the data. It's a bit of a crutch. And whenever you have a hand-engineered step like that, the specific choices you make end up mattering a lot, because the model can't easily undo them.

You see the consequences everywhere. Things like how numbers get split, how whitespace is handled, why models struggle with spelling or counting letters in a word, performance gaps across languages that happen to be tokenized less efficiently. A lot of those quirks trace back to the tokenizer rather than anything fundamental about language or about learning.

So from my perspective, the fact that the tokenizer matters so much is really a symptom. It tells you there's a piece of the modeling problem that the architecture has outsourced. And that's part of what's motivated some of my own work on alternative sequence models and on hierarchical or multi-scale approaches. The question I keep coming back to is: can we build architectures that learn that chunking end to end, so the model figures out what the right units are from the data itself, rather than us baking in a fixed vocabulary up front? If you can do that, you not only get rid of a whole class of weird failure modes, but I think you also get a model that scales more gracefully to things like raw bytes, code, or other modalities where a handcrafted tokenizer is much less natural to begin with.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tokenization choices and their effects, but does not describe a shift from separate word-level and character-level regimes to treating tokenization as a model hyperparameter.

r002.rationale: It says Transformers work well with discrete, meaningful units and that tokenization supplies those units before the model sees the data, expressing dependence on tokens that already encode meaningful structure.

astra-6.text:
I think tokenization is one of those things that we tend to treat as a preprocessing detail, but it actually changes the problem the model has to solve. It determines what the model sees as a single unit, how long the sequence is, and how much structure has already been built into the input before the model ever sees it.

For a Transformer, that sequence length is particularly important because attention has a quadratic cost. If you operate on bytes or characters, you get much longer sequences, and that becomes expensive. So tokenization is partly a way of compressing the sequence into something the architecture can handle efficiently.

But that also introduces a particular bias. Common words might be represented as one token, while less common words get broken into several pieces. Numbers, different languages, and code can all get split in ways that affect how easy they are to learn. And even a small change in the text can change the segmentation.

So the tokenizer isn't just an implementation choice. It's tied to both the computational constraints of the architecture and the representations the model can learn. One question that interests me is whether, with architectures that handle long sequences more efficiently, we can do less of that preprocessing and let the model learn more directly from the raw data.

r001.rationale: The response says tokenization is more than an implementation choice, but does not identify a shift from distinct word- and character-level regimes to treating tokenization as a model hyperparameter.

r002.rationale: It notes that tokenization builds structure into inputs and affects representations, but does not propose that Transformer sensitivity stems from reliance on tokens that already encode meaningful units.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tokenizer is one of those things that we sometimes treat as preprocessing, but it’s really part of the model. It determines what the model sees as a single step, and that affects both what it can learn easily and how expensive it is to run.

If you work directly with bytes or characters, you have a very simple, general representation, but your sequences get much longer. And that’s particularly expensive for a Transformer because of the cost of attention. So tokenization is doing a kind of compression: you pack common sequences into individual tokens so the Transformer has fewer steps to process.

But you’re also imposing a particular structure on the data. Two very similar strings can get split into quite different tokens, and something that’s one token in one language might take several in another. So it affects efficiency, but also how the model generalizes. Ideally, you’d like the model to learn those useful abstractions itself, rather than having so much depend on this fixed preprocessing choice.

r002.rationale: The response says tokenization packs common sequences into tokens and affects learning and generalization, but does not propose that Transformers’ sensitivity reflects dependence on tokens that already encode meaningful units.
